strengths: Addresses a clear and practical problem: multi-token prediction (MTP) speeds up structured language model inference for 3D layout estimation but suffers accuracy degradation; the paper proposes concrete solutions (SSD adaptation, CGD, parameter-efficient sharing) to mitigate this.

The proposed confidence-guided decoding (CGD) is a reasonable extension of scoring-based token filtering, with an ablation showing it outperforms prior ProductThre/SoftmaxThre baselines in accepted-token rate and accuracy.

Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 3) isolate the effect of the numerical-token distance metric, parameter sharing, and different filtering strategies, and the softmax-score analysis (Fig. 8) gives useful insight into why raw softmax confidence is an unreliable filtering signal.

Reported results show a favorable trade-off: comparable or better F1-score than SceneScript with ~5x latency reduction and much smaller parameter overhead than naive MTP, evaluated consistently across two datasets (ASE, Structured3D) with both val/test splits.

The adaptation of self-speculative decoding with a distance-based tolerance for numerical tokens is a sensible, task-specific modification that is empirically validated to improve acceptance rate without accuracy loss.
weaknesses: The core techniques (MTP, self-speculative decoding, confidence/scoring-based filtering, head-sharing efficiency tricks) are largely adapted from existing LLM literature (DeepSeek-V3, Medusa, SSD, VocalNet, etc.); the technical novelty is primarily in domain adaptation rather than new algorithmic ideas, which limits the originality contribution.

Evaluation is restricted to a single downstream task (3D scene layout estimation) and a single base architecture (SceneScript), despite the paper's framing around "perception-generalist" language models and mention of other 3D tasks (object detection, part reconstruction) that are never tested; this narrows the generality claims.

No comparison against SpatialLM, another closely related generalist 3D structured language model discussed in related work, leaving open whether the proposed acceleration techniques transfer beyond SceneScript.

Latency is measured only on a relatively dated GPU (RTX 2080 Ti) without batch-inference or modern-hardware analysis, and no wall-clock comparison of end-to-end pipeline (including encoder) is given, which could affect the practical significance of the claimed speedups.

Hyperparameters (τ for SSD tolerance, ϵ threshold for CGD, λh, λc) appear to be manually tuned with limited sensitivity analysis beyond a few values in the supplementary, raising minor reproducibility concerns.

Both benchmark datasets (ASE, Structured3D) are synthetic/simulated; no evaluation on real-world captured point clouds is provided to demonstrate robustness to sensor noise, which is relevant for the claimed robotics/AR applications.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practical problem: accelerating autoregressive structured-language decoding for 3D scene layout estimation, which is important for real-time robotics/AR applications.

The combination of multi-token prediction with two complementary token-filtering strategies (SSD adapted with a numerical distance tolerance, and a novel confidence-guided decoding scheme) is a sensible and reasonably novel adaptation of LLM acceleration techniques to structured, deterministic output spaces.

The parameter-efficient head-sharing/projection-block design meaningfully reduces the overhead of MTP heads (~43% fewer parameters than naive MTP) while largely preserving accuracy, which is a useful practical contribution.

Experiments are conducted on two datasets (ASE and Structured3D) with consistent latency, parameter count, F1-score, and acceptance-rate (alpha) metrics, and include an ablation table isolating the effect of tau, parameter sharing, and different filtering strategies (SSD vs. CGD vs. ProductThre vs. SoftmaxThre).
Qualitative visualizations and token-acceptance/softmax-score distribution analyses (Fig. 7, 8) provide some interpretability for why CGD/SSD outperform naive confidence thresholding.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination/adaptation of existing techniques (MTP from Gloeckle et al., self-speculative decoding, Medusa-style multi-head prediction, confidence-based early exit) applied to an existing architecture (SceneScript); the novelty is incremental rather than a fundamentally new method, and this is not sufficiently acknowledged or contrasted against closely related speculative-decoding scoring baselines beyond a narrow ablation.

Evaluation is restricted to a single base architecture (SceneScript) and a single task (layout estimation with only wall/window/door categories); no evidence is given that the approach generalizes to SceneScript's other claimed tasks (3D object detection, part reconstruction) or to SpatialLM-style large decoder backbones, despite the introduction motivating the work with broader perception-generalist claims.

Latency is measured only on a single, relatively old GPU (RTX 2080 Ti) with no discussion of batch size, precision, or variance across runs; no wall-clock breakdown of encoder vs. decoder cost, and no comparison of end-to-end (encoder+decoder) latency, which limits reproducibility and practical relevance to modern hardware.

Hyperparameter choices (tau=2, epsilon threshold for CGD, ProductThre/SoftmaxThre thresholds of 0.3/0.5) appear tuned specifically to maximize speed at matched accuracy without clear justification of how these were selected or their sensitivity, raising concerns about cherry-picking and limiting reproducibility.

The accuracy 'improvement' over plain SceneScript (NTP) on Structured3D (+2.07% F1) is attributed to MTP regularization effects analogous to DeepSeek-V3, but this claim is not rigorously tested (e.g., no controlled study isolating whether gains come from the confidence auxiliary loss, MTP-induced regularization, or dataset-specific noise), especially given the small Structured3D test set (250 scenes).

The paper does not report variance/multiple seeds for any experiment, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (e.g., 12.04% F1 over MTP baseline, 5.09x speedup) are statistically meaningful or within noise, particularly given relatively small test sets.

The confidence head training signal (agreement with the first head's prediction under a distance threshold) creates a somewhat circular reliability definition — confidence is calibrated to match the first head rather than to ground truth correctness, which is a conceptual limitation not discussed or ablated against a ground-truth-supervised alternative.

Presentation issues: Figure 1 compares only against MTP variants with n=4,8,10 but the text's headline claims (12.04% F1, 43% fewer parameters, 5.09x speedup) refer to different specific row comparisons in Tables 1/2 that are not always clearly cross-referenced in the abstract/intro, which could mislead readers about the generality of these numbers.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: accelerating autoregressive structured language models for 3D scene layout estimation, where inference latency scales poorly with sequence length.

The combination of multi-token prediction with a token filtering mechanism (SSD and the novel CGD) is well motivated and directly targets the accuracy degradation that typically accompanies MTP, which is empirically demonstrated in Tables 1-2 (e.g., naive MTP drops F1 by ~11% while Fast SceneScript nearly matches NTP accuracy).

The parameter-efficient head-sharing mechanism is a sensible and effective contribution, reducing decoder parameters by ~43-48% relative to standard MTP heads with negligible accuracy loss (Table 3, rows d vs f, i vs j), addressing a real practical concern for MTP-based approaches.

The augmentation of SSD with a distance-based tolerance for numerical tokens (Eq. 3) is a reasonable structured-language-specific adaptation with a clear ablation (Table 3, rows c-e) showing improved throughput.

Reasonably thorough experimental evaluation across two datasets (ASE, Structured3D) with consistent latency, parameter count, accuracy, and average accepted token count (α) metrics, plus qualitative comparisons and token acceptance/softmax-score distribution analyses (Fig. 7, 8) that support the claim that softmax confidence alone is an unreliable acceptance criterion.
Comparison against RoomFormer and against vanilla MTP baselines with varying n provides useful context for the trade-offs achieved.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: MTP, self-speculative decoding, and confidence/score-based token filtering are all adapted from existing LLM literature (DeepSeek-V3, Medusa, SSD works, DynaMo/scoring papers) rather than fundamentally new mechanisms; the core innovation is largely in combining and tailoring these techniques to structured 3D layout tokens.

Latency is measured only on a single, relatively dated GPU (RTX 2080 Ti) without reporting variance across hardware, batch sizes, or newer accelerators, which limits confidence in how the reported speedups generalize.

The method is evaluated only on the layout-estimation task within SceneScript-style pipelines; although the abstract/intro position this as broadly applicable to language-based perception generalist models (e.g., 3D object detection, part reconstruction), no experiments on those other tasks are shown, so the generality claim is not empirically substantiated.

Hyperparameter choices (τ=2, ϵ threshold for CGD, λh, λc) appear tuned on ASE and are not clearly justified with sensitivity analysis in the main text (some deferred to supplementary), leaving open how sensitive the method is to these settings across datasets/domains.

The comparison baselines for scoring-based filtering (ProductThre, SoftmaxThre) are adapted from unrelated domains (diffusion LMs) with thresholds manually set to 'maximize speed without compromising accuracy,' which could bias the comparison in favor of CGD if baseline thresholds were not equally optimized.

Structured3D results show relatively higher latency variability and only modest α for CGD (e.g., 6.15-7.15) compared to SSD, and the paper does not fully analyze why CGD sometimes underperforms SSD in speed despite claiming on-the-fly decoding advantages.

Reproducibility could be improved: some training details (e.g., exact confidence threshold ϵ) and further ablations on n are relegated to supplementary material not included here, making full independent verification from the main text alone difficult.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: the high latency of autoregressive next-token prediction in structured language models for 3D scene understanding.

Extensive empirical validation across three datasets (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD) and two tasks (layout estimation, object detection), with consistent speedups (5.09x-5.57x) while matching or exceeding SceneScript accuracy.

Thorough ablation studies covering hyperparameters (tau, epsilon), the parameter-sharing mechanism, and comparisons against alternative scoring-based filtering baselines (ProductThre, SoftmaxThre), supported by detailed distribution analyses (Fig. 6, 7, S2-S4).

The proposed adaptation of self-speculative decoding with a numerical-token distance metric and the confidence-guided decoding (CGD) mechanism are sensible, task-specific design choices that show measurable benefit over generic scoring baselines.
Parameter-efficient head-sharing mechanism substantially reduces MTP overhead (43% fewer parameters) with negligible accuracy loss, which is a useful practical contribution.
Reasonably clear presentation with good figures illustrating the decoding process and comprehensive supplementary material with failure-case analysis.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination and adaptation of existing techniques (MTP from Gloeckle et al., self-speculative decoding, confidence/threshold-based early exit decoding common in NLP), rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; novelty is incremental within a narrow domain (SceneScript-style tokenized 3D scenes).

CGD confidence labels are generated by comparing against the first head's own prediction rather than ground truth, which could propagate first-head errors into the confidence signal; the paper acknowledges comparable but not superior accuracy versus the GT-supervised variant without deeper analysis of when/why first-head errors matter.

Latency is measured only on an old GPU (RTX 2080 Ti) with no discussion of batch size, hardware generality, or comparison to other acceleration paradigms (e.g., actual draft-model speculative decoding, parallel decoding outside the MTP framework).

Object detection evaluation on ASE relies on pseudo-ground-truth bounding boxes generated by an off-the-shelf detector (TR3D) rather than true annotations, and is restricted to only 5 common object categories, limiting the strength of the object detection claims.
SceneCAD training set is very small (~1k scenes), and the reported gains there, while presented as evidence of real-world applicability, may not generalize robustly given the limited data.
No statistical significance testing or repeated-run variance reporting is provided for the main comparisons, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported percentage improvements.

The method's applicability appears fairly specific to SceneScript-like structured sequence formats; broader claims about general language-based perception generalists are not empirically tested beyond this one family of models.

strengths: Addresses a practically important bottleneck (slow autoregressive decoding) in language-based 3D scene understanding models such as SceneScript, which is a timely and relevant problem for the perception-generalist trend.

The combination of multi-token prediction with a token-filtering mechanism tailored to structured languages (distance-based tolerance for numerical tokens in SSD, and a confidence head supervised by consistency with the first head rather than ground truth) is a sensible domain adaptation that is empirically shown to outperform naive MTP and generic softmax/cumulative-probability thresholding baselines.

The parameter-efficient head-sharing/projection-block design is a clean, well-motivated contribution that achieves a large (~43%) reduction in decoder parameters relative to standard MTP heads while largely preserving accuracy (Table 4, rows i vs j).

Experimental coverage is relatively broad: three datasets (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD), two tasks (layout estimation and object detection), and several ablations (τ, ϵ thresholds, number of heads, confidence-label supervision strategy, with/without parameter sharing), which supports the main claims reasonably well.
The softmax-score analysis (Fig. 7, Fig. S2) is a nice piece of evidence showing that naive softmax-based filtering is a poor proxy for token reliability, supporting the motivation for CGD.
Qualitative results and failure-case analysis are included, adding some transparency about where the method struggles (incomplete point clouds, non-Manhattan layouts).
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is incremental: MTP, self-speculative decoding, and confidence/threshold-based token filtering are all adopted largely unmodified from prior NLP work (Gloeckle et al., Medusa, VocalNet, speculative decoding literature); the contribution here is primarily domain adaptation (numerical-token tolerance, head-sharing) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, which somewhat undercuts the claim of being 'the first work to introduce MTP to language-based perception models.'

Fairness of the main comparison is unclear: Table S5 shows that simply training the SceneScript NTP baseline longer (90 vs 60 epochs) already closes much of the reported accuracy gap/improvement (0.915→0.920 mean F1), raising the question of whether Fast SceneScript's reported accuracy gains over SceneScript are attributable to the proposed method or to training/regularization effects not controlled for across baselines.

Latency is measured only on a single, relatively old GPU (RTX 2080 Ti) with batch size apparently 1; no analysis of how the speedup scales with batching, on modern hardware, or under realistic deployment settings, limiting the practical significance of the reported speedups.

Many reported accuracy improvements are small in absolute terms (e.g., mean F1 0.911 vs 0.913, or 0.908 vs 0.911 across filtering variants) and no variance/multiple-seed results are reported, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the comparisons used to justify design choices (e.g., CGD vs SSD vs ProductThre vs SoftmaxThre).

The object-detection evaluation on ASE relies on pseudo ground-truth bounding boxes generated by a separate off-the-shelf detector (TR3D) rather than official annotations, which introduces an additional source of label noise/bias that is not discussed as a limitation.

The method is validated only on a relatively small, task-specific decoder (14M parameters) built on SceneScript's bespoke structured language; it remains unclear whether the approach generalizes to larger, more general-purpose LLM-based 3D perception systems (e.g., SpatialLM, which uses a full LLM backbone), limiting the claimed generality as a 'perception-generalist' acceleration technique.

The ablations comparing CGD/SSD against baseline scoring methods (ProductThre, SoftmaxThre) use thresholds tuned specifically for this setting without a principled selection procedure, and no hybrid or alternative combinations (e.g., combining SSD and CGD) are explored, leaving open whether the reported gains are an artifact of threshold tuning rather than a fundamentally better reliability signal.

The paper's claimed contributions (speed, accuracy, parameter efficiency) are somewhat overlapping/intertwined across three components (MTP, filtering, parameter sharing), and the paper does not clearly isolate how much of the overall improvement stems from each individual component versus their combination, beyond the single ablation table on ASE val set.

strengths: First work to introduce multi-token prediction (MTP) into structured language models for 3D scene understanding, addressing an important latency bottleneck for autoregressive perception-generalist models.

Two complementary token-filtering strategies are proposed: an SSD variant with a task-specific tolerance (distance metric) for numerical tokens, and a novel confidence-guided decoding (CGD) scheme that enables single-pass, on-the-fly verification instead of requiring an extra verification iteration.

A lightweight, head-sharing parameter-efficient projection mechanism reduces the parameter overhead of adding extra MTP heads by ~43-48% relative to naive multi-head MTP, while largely preserving accuracy.

Extensive empirical validation across three datasets (synthetic ASE, synthetic Structured3D, real-world SceneCAD) and two tasks (layout estimation, object detection), with consistent large latency reductions (5.09x-5.57x) and accuracy that is comparable to or better than the NTP baseline, and clearly superior to naive MTP.

Useful diagnostic analyses (Fig. 6, Fig. 7, and supplementary Fig. S2/S4) showing that raw softmax confidence is a poor proxy for token reliability, motivating the design of CGD; ablations on τ, ϵ, number of heads, and head-sharing are thorough and support the design choices.
Comparison against a specialized non-LM baseline (RoomFormer) contextualizes the accuracy/speed trade-off of the unified language-model approach.
weaknesses: The core techniques (multi-token prediction with auxiliary heads, self-speculative decoding, confidence/threshold-based early stopping) are all adapted from existing NLP/LLM literature; the main novelty lies in domain-specific adaptations (numeric-token tolerance, head-sharing projection, confidence supervision from first-head consistency) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea, making the contribution more incremental/engineering-oriented.

CGD's practical latency benefit over SSD is not clearly established: in several tables (e.g., Table 1, Row f vs g; Table 2, Row f vs g) CGD is consistently slower than SSD despite accepting fewer tokens per iteration on average, which seems to undercut the claimed advantage of removing verification delay; this trade-off is not discussed in the text.

Latency is measured on an aging RTX 2080 Ti with (implicitly) batch size 1; it is unclear how the reported speedups and absolute latencies (tens to hundreds of ms) translate to modern hardware or to batched/streaming inference scenarios relevant for real applications.

Threshold hyperparameters (τ for SSD/CGD supervision, ϵ for CGD stopping) appear to require per-setting tuning, and the paper does not discuss sensitivity to unseen scene distributions or the cost of retuning for new datasets/tasks.

The claimed generality of the framework (applicable to layout estimation, object detection, and "3D object part reconstruction") is only empirically validated on two of these tasks; no evaluation of part reconstruction is presented despite being referenced as a use case.

SceneCAD evaluation relies on a very small training set (~1k scenes), and combined with the ASE detection annotations being pseudo-labels generated by a separate detector (TR3D) rather than ground truth, the object-detection accuracy numbers rest on a somewhat indirect evaluation protocol whose reliability is not thoroughly discussed.

No direct comparison to SpatialLM, the other prominent language-based 3D generalist model discussed in related work, leaving open how the proposed acceleration techniques would generalize beyond SceneScript's specific decoder architecture.
